sources.title: OpenAI Help Center: Understanding and counting tokens
sources.note: Primary source for what a token is, that counts differ by model, encoding and language, that token IDs depend on the encoding, the Tokenizer tool, and that the context window limits tokens. Read 2026-10-20 (page shows a relative 'Updated' date only).

sources.title: tiktoken README (OpenAI)
sources.note: Primary source for 'language models see sequences of numbers (tokens)' and how byte pair encoding turns text into tokens. Read 2026-10-20.

sources.title: Hugging Face Transformers: Tokenization algorithms
sources.note: Documentation of BPE, byte-level BPE, Unigram and WordPiece; lists Qwen2 among BPE models. Read 2026-10-20.

sources.title: Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units (Sennrich, Haddow, Birch)
sources.note: Original paper applying byte pair encoding to subword units (arXiv v5 dated 2016-06-10; first submitted 2015-08-31). Used only for the idea of subword pieces.

sources.title: OpenAI Tokenizer (web tool)
sources.note: Named as the tool for seeing how text is divided in source 1. Not opened or run by this work; recorded only as the example of a model provider's own tokenizer.

claims.text: A token can be a character, part of a word, a whole word or punctuation, and spaces also affect how text is divided.
claims.evidence: OpenAI Help Center, Overview: 'A token can represent a character, part of a word, a whole word, or punctuation. Spaces also affect how text is divided into tokens.'
claims.caveat: Stated for OpenAI models; the splits shown in the video come from a different tokenizer.

claims.text: A token count is not the same as a word count; the same text can give different counts depending on the model, its encoding and the language.
claims.evidence: OpenAI Help Center, Overview: 'A token count is not the same as a word count. The same text can produce different token counts depending on the model, its encoding, and the language.'

claims.text: Token IDs depend on the encoding; an example ID does not apply to every model.
claims.evidence: OpenAI Help Center: 'Token IDs also depend on the encoding. Do not assume that an example token ID applies to every model.'
claims.caveat: The IDs on screen are labelled as belonging to the named tokenizer.

claims.text: Language models work on sequences of numbers (tokens); byte pair encoding converts text into tokens, can be reversed exactly, and lets the model see common subwords.
claims.evidence: tiktoken README: 'Language models don't see text like you and I, instead they see a sequence of numbers (known as tokens)... It's reversible and lossless... It attempts to let the model see common subwords.' Hugging Face docs describe BPE and byte-level BPE.
claims.caveat: Describes BPE tokenizers; other tokenizer designs (Unigram, WordPiece) cut text differently.

claims.text: With the Qwen3-TTS text tokenizer (byte-level BPE (Qwen2Tokenizer)), the message 'Remind me to recharge my Jio plan tomorrow' is 8 words and 10 tokens: Rem | ind | ·me | ·to | ·recharge | ·my | ·J | io | ·plan | ·tomorrow (a dot marks a leading space).
claims.evidence: Measured: samples/ai-maxxing-01/tokenizer-evidence.json (decode of the ids reproduces the exact text).
claims.caveat: One tokenizer of one model family. Another model will cut this text differently.

claims.text: With the same tokenizer, 'Wake me at six tomorrow morning' is 6 tokens and a Hindi version of the request is 23 tokens.
claims.caveat: One sentence pair on one tokenizer; not a general ratio. The Hindi wording was written for this episode and should be checked by a fluent reader before publishing.

claims.text: The context window limits the tokens a model can work with in a request; check your model's documentation for its limit.
claims.evidence: OpenAI Help Center, 'Stay within model limits'.

claims.text: Before pasting a long prompt, check its token count with your model's tokenizer.
claims.evidence: Practical takeaway drawn from the Help Center's 'Count tokens before sending a request' (Tokenizer tool, tiktoken).
claims.caveat: Not every app exposes a tokenizer or token counter, and a plain-text count does not include everything in an API request.
